t: Count the Number of K-Big Indices
o: Index i is k-big if at least k indices before it hold strictly smaller values AND at least k indices after it hold strictly smaller values. For each i we therefore need leftSmaller(i) and rightSmaller(i) — the classic 'count smaller elements to the left' problem solved with a Fenwick tree over value ranks. In [2,3,6,5,2,3], k=2: index 2 (value 6) has {2,3} before and {5,2,3} after → both ≥ 2 ✓; index 3 (value 5) has {2,3} before and {2,3} after ✓; answer 2. n up to 1e5 requires the O(n log n) BIT; a merge-sort counting variant also works.
k: Compute leftSmaller and rightSmaller independently with a BIT, then count indices where both are ≥ k.
Strict inequality means query the prefix count of values < nums[i] (rank nums[i]-1).

a.i: Sweep left to right: before inserting nums[i], query how many inserted values are < nums[i] — that's leftSmaller[i]. Sweep right to left identically for rightSmaller[i]. Count positions where both ≥ k.
s: Build a BIT sized to max(nums).
Left sweep: query prefix(nums[i]-1), store, then insert nums[i].
Answer = #{i : left[i] ≥ k and right[i] ≥ k}.
a.t: O(n log V) — two BIT sweeps with log V per operation

a.i: Run merge-sort-based counting twice (once on the array, once on the reversed array) to obtain, for each element, the number of strictly smaller elements preceding it. During merge, for each element of the left half count right-half elements smaller than it via a pointer; add to that element's tally. Combine tallies from both directions and count qualifying indices.
s: Merge-sort count smaller-to-the-left on nums → left[].
Same on reversed nums → right[] (reversed back).
Count i with left[i] ≥ k and right[i] ≥ k.
a.t: O(n log n) — two merge-sort counting passes

w: The BIT sweep is shorter and less error-prone; merge sort avoids value-domain sizing if values were huge (here they're bounded by n anyway). Strictness matters: query rank nums[i]-1, not nums[i], or equal elements get miscounted. Edge cases: k larger than any achievable side count → 0; duplicated values handled naturally by the strict comparison. Follow-up: report the indices themselves, or handle a stream with updates (BIT adapts, merge sort does not).
